archetype.name: Rebuilding (run-first, broken back end)
archetype.definition: A third straight bottom-tier Titans team that can move the ball in steady, run-leaning drives but has a pass defense that gives up the most explosive throws in the league, so it loses shootouts it can't keep pace in.

report.headline: The offense has found a pulse; the pass defense is giving games away.
report.take:
This is the third consecutive year the Titans have lived at the bottom of the league. They won 3 games in both 2024 and 2025, and at 1-9 with a -93 point differential they are on the same track. Robert Saleh is not new and Cam Ward has started every game, so the season can't be explained by a quarterback carousel or a coaching reset. What the film and the numbers show is a team in two halves that rarely play well on the same afternoon. Its net EPA ranks 28th.

The offense is the more coherent half. It runs more than the situation calls for (pass rate over expected -3.7, 26th), and Tony Pollard has carried the ball far more than anyone else. The line keeps Ward clean once the ball is out: 13 sacks allowed ranks 5th. The unit stays on schedule with a success rate 13th in the league. What it lacks is a payoff. Pass EPA ranks 24th and yardage 31st, and the Titans hold the ball less than any team in football (25.63 minutes, 32nd). On defense the front does its job, with a 4th-ranked pressure rate and the 2nd-lowest missed-tackle rate. Behind it, the coverage gives up explosive passes at the league's worst rate and pass EPA ranks 31st. Opposing WR1s are scoring 6.4 PPR points a game over their norm, 31st.

The record is a little harsher than the play. The point differential implies about 2.5 wins, and a 0.167 win rate in one-score games (28th) has cost them at least one result. The more telling story is the last four games. The offense scored 24, 36, 23 and 30, its best stretch of the year, while the defense allowed 27, 43, 40 and 51. Cincinnati threw for 462 yards and Jacksonville for 352. Opponents actually run against Tennessee more than usual (pass rate over norm -4, a run funnel), likely because they are protecting leads. That means the secondary is being torched on a modest number of throws, which is worse, not better.

Where it goes from here depends on whether the secondary can be stabilized. Cor'Dale Flott and two safeties left the Dallas game hurt, and an injury-thinned back end facing a 7th-ranked passing offense is the worst version of this matchup. The back half of the schedule has softer spots: Indianapolis with the 31st-ranked offense, Las Vegas and Washington. A second and maybe third win is realistic. The ceiling is a competitive December, not a turnaround.

strengths.title: A pass rush that gets home
strengths.body: The front generates pressure at the 4th-best rate in the league and tackles cleanly behind it, with only Saleh-style discipline showing up as a missed-tackle rate ranked 2nd. The weakness is conversion: pressure has turned into an ordinary sack rate. The six-sack day at Indianapolis shows what it looks like when it finishes. This is the most durable thing about the defense and does not depend on the injured secondary.

strengths.title: An offense that stays on schedule
strengths.body: Tennessee's offensive success rate ranks 13th, the line's yards before contact rank 10th, and the backs are rarely stuffed. That is a functional early-down operation, not a broken one. Ward has also limited sacks despite a high pressure rate allowed. The offense has scored 23 or more in four straight games, so the floor is rising even if the explosiveness isn't there.

strengths.title: Run defense holds the line
strengths.body: Against the run the Titans are roughly league average: 15th in rush EPA allowed and 6th in rushing touchdowns allowed per game. Opponents do run against them more than usual, but mostly while protecting leads, and the run fit has held up. The pass defense is losing games; the run defense is not.

concerns.title: Coverage gives up the big play
concerns.body: No defense allows explosive passes more often (32nd), and pass EPA allowed per play ranks 31st. Opposing top receivers feast: their EPA per target against Tennessee ranks 30th. The pressure up front isn't buying enough time for this secondary. With Flott and safeties Tony Adams and Terrell Burgess all leaving the Dallas game hurt, it can get worse before it gets better.

concerns.title: A passing game without a punch
concerns.body: Ward's passing EPA ranks 24th and the offense gains the 31st-most yards per game. The line allows pressure at the 30th-ranked rate even though it limits sacks. Combined with a run-first lean, the result is long, low-yield possessions and the league's lowest time of possession. That leaves the defense on the field too long and gives the offense too few chances to answer.

concerns.title: Close games keep slipping away
concerns.body: Tennessee is 28th in one-score win rate. The turnover margin has drifted negative, 14 giveaways against 12 takeaways, with two-turnover games common. Part of this is bad luck: the differential implies 2.5 wins. A team this short on explosive plays, though, can't afford a single giveaway in a tight game.

trend.note: The offense has climbed to its best scoring of the year over the last four games, but the defense has collapsed in the same span, allowing 43, 40 and 51 in the last three. Results haven't changed: every game since the Week 6 win at Indianapolis is a loss.

nextGame.headline: Back to Jacksonville, where the secondary got torched two weeks ago
nextGame.body:
Two weeks ago Jacksonville won 40-23 in Nashville, throwing for 352 yards. Little about this rematch favors Tennessee. The Jaguars are 2nd in net EPA, 1st in point differential per game and 1st in turnover margin. Their defense is built to erase exactly what the Titans do well: it ranks 1st against the run by EPA and 1st against short passes, and it smothers tight ends and lead backs. The Book has Jacksonville -14.5 with a 47.5 total and Tennessee at +760. The cracks are real but narrow. Jacksonville's defense ranks 21st on deep passes, has been beaten by slot and third receivers (WR3 PPR over average 31st), and finishes few of its pressures (sack rate 30th). The Jaguars also come off a 23-18 loss to the Giants.

Availability matters on both sides. Left tackle Dan Moore Jr. (96% of snaps) is questionable with a knee injury, and his absence would expose a line that already allows pressure at the 30th-ranked rate. Corner Cor'Dale Flott (89%) is questionable with a neck injury, and safeties Tony Adams and Terrell Burgess are questionable after leaving the Dallas game. A depleted back end against Trevor Lawrence is the nightmare scenario. Tyjae Spears is on IR, so the backfield is Pollard's alone. For Jacksonville, center Robert Hainsey (91%) is out and tackle Walker Little is questionable, which gives the Titans' pass rush its best opening. Corner Jarrian Jones and back Bhayshul Tuten are also questionable, and two rotational edge rushers are out.

waysToWin.title: Pressure a line missing its center
waysToWin.body: Tennessee's pressure rate ranks 4th and Jacksonville is without its starting center, with Walker Little questionable. Collapsing the pocket is the one way to keep Lawrence from reaching the secondary. This front has done it before: six sacks and three takeaways in the Indianapolis win.

waysToWin.title: Take deep shots and target the third receiver
waysToWin.body: Jacksonville is airtight underneath but 21st on deep throws, and its coverage of third receivers ranks near the bottom. Ward needs Elic Ayomanor and a couple of downfield throws to hit. Jacksonville pressures without finishing, which gives those routes time to develop if Moore plays.

waysToWin.title: Win the turnover battle outright
waysToWin.body: A two-touchdown underdog needs extra possessions. Tennessee has had multi-takeaway games, including four at Cincinnati, and Jacksonville's offense will be running behind a patched-up interior. Anything short of a plus margin probably isn't enough.

waysToLose.title: Lawrence finds the explosive throws again
waysToLose.body: Jacksonville's 7th-ranked passing offense meets the league's most explosive-pass-prone defense, and the secondary may be missing a starting corner and two safeties. The last meeting produced 352 passing yards. A repeat ends this early.

waysToLose.title: The run-first plan hits a wall
waysToLose.body: Tennessee leans on Pollard and short throws. Jacksonville is 1st in rush EPA allowed and 1st against short passes, and it shuts down lead backs and tight ends. If early downs fail, the Titans are in obvious passing situations behind a line that allows pressure at the 30th-ranked rate.

waysToLose.title: Giveaways feed the league's best margin
waysToLose.body: Jacksonville leads the league in turnover differential and has the 3rd-most takeaways. Tennessee has turned it over in every game but one. Short fields would turn a likely loss into a rout.

nextGame.watch: Whether Flott and the safeties play, and whether the Titans' pass rush can collapse a Jaguars pocket missing its center before Lawrence gets to the deep middle.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense's recent scoring is partly real and partly opponent-driven. Dallas and Cincinnati were shootouts against defenses that let points pile up, but the steady success rate and the line's sack avoidance give the unit a reasonable floor near 20 points. The defense is the problem. It allowed 29 points per game across the season and much more lately, and a secondary this explosive-prone, now dealing with injuries, won't fix itself in-season. Expect points allowed to stay high against Detroit and Houston, and offer a little relief against Indianapolis's 31st-ranked offense.

The one-score luck should even out somewhat. The differential suggests the Titans have been closer to a 2-3 win team than a one-win team. Combined with home games against Washington and Indianapolis and a trip to Las Vegas, which ranks 28th on defense, one or two more wins are likely. More than that requires the pass defense to stop leaking.
swingFactors: Health of the secondary (Flott, Adams, Burgess)
Dan Moore Jr.'s knee and Ward's protection

confidence.note: Ten games with one quarterback make a clear profile, but secondary injuries and a sharp defensive slide add uncertainty.
